subject: Biology
description: Plant reproduction — sexual (flowers, pollination, fertilization), asexual (vegetative propagation), seeds, fruits, double fertilization.

questions.stem: POLLINATION is the transfer of pollen from anther to:
questions.explanation: POLLINATION — transfer of pollen grains from MALE part (ANTHER, top of stamen) to FEMALE part (STIGMA, top of pistil/carpel). FLOWER STRUCTURE: (1) STAMENS (male) — anther + filament. (2) PISTIL/CARPEL (female) — STIGMA (sticky top) + STYLE (tube) + OVARY (containing ovules). (3) PETALS — colored, attract pollinators. (4) SEPALS — green, protect bud. TYPES OF POLLINATION: (1) SELF-POLLINATION — pollen from same flower → genetic uniformity. (2) CROSS-POLLINATION — pollen from another flower of same species → genetic diversity. AGENTS OF POLLINATION (POLLINATORS): (a) INSECTS — bees, butterflies, moths (most flowers). (b) BIRDS — humming birds, sunbirds (red flowers, no scent). (c) BATS — for night-blooming flowers (saguaro cactus, baobab). (d) WIND — grasses, conifers, oaks (small/no petals, lots of pollen, high in air). (e) WATER — aquatic plants. INDIAN POLLINATORS: ~200 species of bees; honey bees Apis mellifera, A. dorsata (rock bee), A. cerana (Indian hive bee). DECLINE in pollinators due to pesticides, habitat loss, climate change → MAJOR CONCERN for global food security. PYQ FREQUENCY: pollination basics in NEET, NCERT 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: DOUBLE FERTILIZATION is a unique feature of:
questions.explanation: DOUBLE FERTILIZATION — UNIQUE to ANGIOSPERMS (flowering plants). Discovered by S. NAWASCHIN (1898, Russian botanist). PROCESS: pollen grain on stigma germinates into a POLLEN TUBE that grows down style to ovule. TWO MALE GAMETES are released: (1) ONE male gamete fuses with EGG (n) → ZYGOTE (2n) → embryo. (2) OTHER male gamete fuses with TWO POLAR NUCLEI (in central cell, n+n) → TRIPLE FUSION (3n endosperm) → ENDOSPERM (nutritive tissue feeds embryo). TWO FUSIONS = DOUBLE fertilization. SIGNIFICANCE: (1) ENDOSPERM only forms IF fertilization occurs → energy not wasted on unfertilized seeds. (2) TRIPLOID (3n) endosperm provides RICH NUTRIENTS for embryo development. KINGDOM PLANTAE CLASSIFICATION (memorize): (1) BRYOPHYTES (no vascular tissue, no seeds — mosses, liverworts). (2) PTERIDOPHYTES (vascular, no seeds — ferns, horsetails). (3) GYMNOSPERMS (vascular, naked seeds — pines, cycads). (4) ANGIOSPERMS (vascular, enclosed seeds in fruit — flowering plants; ~270,000 species). ANGIOSPERMS have DOMINATED Earth's flora since CRETACEOUS period; coevolved with insect pollinators. APPLICATION: KNOWING this is critical for plant breeding, hybrid seed production. PYQ FREQUENCY: double fertilization in NEET, NCERT Class 12, AIIMS PG 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Which of these is a method of VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION (asexual reproduction in plants)?
questions.explanation: VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION — ASEXUAL reproduction; new plant arises from PARENT PLANT'S vegetative parts (roots, stems, leaves) — NO seeds, no fertilization. NEW PLANTS are GENETIC CLONES of parent. METHODS: (1) CUTTINGS — stem cuttings rooted in soil (rose, sugar cane, tomatoes, hibiscus, money plant). (2) LAYERING — bending a stem to soil till it roots (jasmine, raspberry). (3) GRAFTING — joining a scion (twig) onto a rootstock (apple, mango, citrus, roses — grown commercially this way). (4) BUDDING — placing a bud onto a rootstock (citrus, peach). (5) RUNNERS / STOLONS — horizontal stems creating new plants (strawberry, mint, grass). (6) RHIZOMES — underground stems (ginger, turmeric, banana). (7) TUBERS — swollen storage stems (potato 'eyes' grow into new plants). (8) SUCKERS — shoots from base (banana). (9) BULBS — onion, garlic, tulip. (10) MICROPROPAGATION (TISSUE CULTURE) — modern lab method; produces 1000s of identical plantlets from a tiny piece (orchid, banana, sugarcane mass production). ADVANTAGES: (a) Fast (skips seed-germination delay). (b) Genetic uniformity (commercial fruit quality). (c) Plant doesn't need pollination. DISADVANTAGES: lack of genetic diversity → vulnerable to disease (e.g., Cavendish banana monoculture is at risk from Panama disease). PYQ FREQUENCY: vegetative propagation in NEET, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The EDIBLE PART of an APPLE is mainly the:
questions.explanation: APPLE — a 'FALSE FRUIT' (or accessory fruit). The fleshy edible part is mostly the THALAMUS (or RECEPTACLE — the swollen base of the flower), not the ovary itself. The actual ovary is the small CORE in the center, containing seeds. TRUE FRUIT vs FALSE FRUIT: (1) TRUE FRUIT — develops from the OVARY only. Examples: mango, tomato, grape, plum, peach, banana, cherry, papaya. (2) FALSE FRUIT (Pseudocarp) — significant edible portion comes from non-ovary tissue (thalamus, calyx, etc.). Examples: APPLE (thalamus), STRAWBERRY (thalamus; the 'seeds' on outside are actually achenes — true fruits), CASHEW (thalamus is the fleshy 'cashew apple'; the nut is the true fruit). FRUIT TYPES: (a) SIMPLE — from one ovary (mango, peach, tomato). (b) AGGREGATE — multiple ovaries from ONE flower (raspberry, blackberry, custard apple). (c) MULTIPLE — multiple flowers (pineapple, jackfruit, mulberry — entire inflorescence). FRUIT FUNCTION: protects seeds, attracts seed-dispersing animals (color, taste, sugar). DISPERSAL MECHANISMS: (1) ANIMAL — eaten + seeds dispersed in feces. (2) WIND — small/winged seeds (dandelion, maple). (3) WATER — coconut, lotus. (4) EXPLOSIVE — pea, balsam. (5) HUMAN — domesticated crops. PYQ FREQUENCY: true vs false fruit in NEET, NCERT Class 12 1× per cycle.

options.option_text: Small, dull flowers, lots of pollen
Large flat petals as landing pads
Closed structure to keep pollen in

questions.explanation: WIND-POLLINATED flowers (ANEMOPHILY) typically have: (1) SMALL, DULL/INCONSPICUOUS flowers (no need to attract animals). (2) NO COLORFUL PETALS, no scent, no nectar. (3) LARGE QUANTITIES of LIGHT, SMOOTH POLLEN (millions of grains; majority lost to wind). (4) Anthers EXPOSED, often DANGLING (catkin-style: birch, willow). (5) STIGMAS LARGE, FEATHERY, EXPOSED to catch wind-borne pollen. (6) FLOWERS often BORNE HIGH on plant for wind exposure. EXAMPLES: most GRASSES (wheat, rice, maize, barley); CONIFERS (pine, fir); MOST TREES (oak, birch, maple, elm); COCONUT (also can be wind+insect). HEALTH IMPACT: wind-pollinated plant POLLEN causes ALLERGIES (hay fever) — RAGWEED, GRASS POLLEN, TREE POLLEN. Pollen-allergy season varies by region. ANIMAL/INSECT-POLLINATED (ENTOMOPHILY) flowers have OPPOSITE features: (1) BRIGHT colored. (2) SCENTED. (3) NECTAR rewards. (4) Sticky pollen with hooks. (5) Specific shape attracts particular pollinators (orchids — co-evolved with specific bees). DARWIN observed an orchid (Angraecum sesquipedale) with a 30-cm nectar tube and predicted a corresponding moth must exist — discovered ~40 years later (Xanthopan praedicta). PYQ FREQUENCY: pollination types in NEET, NCERT 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: After fertilization, the OVULE develops into the:
questions.explanation: AFTER FERTILIZATION: (1) OVULE → SEED (contains embryo, endosperm, seed coat). (2) OVARY → FRUIT (surrounding seeds). (3) Petals, sepals, stamens — usually FALL OFF (some persist in fruit). (4) Stigma + style — wither. SEED ANATOMY: (a) SEED COAT (testa) — protective outer layer, from ovule integuments. (b) EMBRYO — RADICLE (future root), PLUMULE (future shoot), COTYLEDON (1 in monocots, 2 in dicots — seed leaves storing food). (c) ENDOSPERM — nutritive tissue (3n in angiosperms). MONOCOTS (1 cotyledon): rice, wheat, maize, banana, lily, palm, grass. DICOTS (2 cotyledons): bean, pea, mango, neem, sunflower, mustard, most flowering trees. SEED FUNCTIONS: (a) Protect embryo. (b) Store food (cotyledon/endosperm). (c) Disperse to new location. (d) Survive adverse conditions (DORMANCY — seeds can survive years/decades; the OLDEST GERMINATED SEED was a Judaean date palm, 2000 years old). GERMINATION: water uptake → metabolism resumes → radicle emerges first → root → shoot. CONDITIONS: water, oxygen, suitable T (sometimes light/dark). PYQ FREQUENCY: ovule-seed-ovary-fruit relationship in NEET, NCERT 1× per cycle.

questions.explanation: AGAMOSPERMY (or APOMIXIS) — formation of SEEDS WITHOUT FERTILIZATION. Embryo develops directly from a diploid (2n) cell of the ovule (no meiosis, no pollen, no fusion). Result: seed produces a CLONE of the maternal plant. EXAMPLES: (1) MANGO (some varieties). (2) CITRUS (orange, grapefruit, lemon — mostly apomictic; that's why orange seeds breed true to type). (3) GUAVA. (4) DANDELIONS. (5) BLACKBERRIES, BRAMBLES. (6) Some grasses (Pennisetum, Brachiaria). (7) Some Indian crops (rice, wheat) — researched for apomixis to maintain hybrid vigor across generations. ADVANTAGES (for plant + agriculture): (1) Maintains GENOTYPE across generations (no genetic mixing). (2) Hybrid vigor preserved without re-crossing. (3) Faster reproduction. DISADVANTAGES: (1) NO genetic variation → vulnerable to environmental change, disease. RESEARCH: developing apomixis in CEREALS would be REVOLUTIONARY — farmers could replant seeds from hybrid crops without losing yield (currently must buy hybrid seeds yearly). 'POLY-EMBRYONY' often associated — multiple embryos develop in one seed; one is the apomictic clone, others may be sexual. CONTRAST with VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION: agamospermy uses SEEDS (clonal); vegetative uses STEM/ROOT/LEAF cuttings. PYQ FREQUENCY: apomixis in NEET, NCERT Class 12 advanced 1× per cycle.
